clue.text: Where in London the perfect makes practice ?

definitions.text: Where in London the perfect makes practice

parts.words: Where in London the perfect makes practice
parts.note: turns the saying 'practice makes perfect' round: the London street where the most accomplished doctors have their medical practices

explanation.surface: A twist on the proverb, asking where in London the expert sets up shop.
explanation.walkthrough: HARLEY STREET is the London street famous for private doctors' consulting rooms; a doctor's surgery is a 'practice'.
explanation.definitionFit: The street is London's best-known address for eminent private physicians and their practices.

clue.text: Such a rash fellow could be pulled up short.

definitions.text: Such a rash fellow could be pulled up short.

parts.words: Such a rash fellow could be pulled up short
parts.note: a headstrong person, named after a spur used hotly on a horse, which then may be reined in sharply

explanation.surface: A warning that an impetuous man may be brought to a sudden halt.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Percy, nicknamed HOTSPUR in Shakespeare's Henry IV, is the type of the rash young man; a horse given a hot spur may well be pulled up short.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname has become a common noun for any impetuous, headstrong person.

clue.text: Take offence (in two words)

definitions.meaning: to take something is to accept it into your hands
handling stolen goods is a criminal offence known by this verb's -ing form

explanation.walkthrough: '(in two words)' tells you to read 'Take offence' not as the idiom for being upset but as two separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept is to take, and receiving stolen goods is a crime, so the verb fits both halves.

clue.text: But penniless Simon found it difficult, rather.

definitions.text: But penniless Simon found it difficult, rather.

parts.words: But penniless Simon found it difficult, rather
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme Simple Simon had no penny for the pieman's wares, so for him the phrase meaning very simple was ironically untrue

explanation.surface: A remark that a broke man called Simon struggled with a task.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, Simple Simon asks the pieman for a taste but has 'not any' penny, so a pie was far from easy for him to get.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for very simple, and the clue's irony says penniless Simon found the pie anything but.

clue.text: Used needle. to destroy weeds

indicators.note: destroying the word weeds breaks it apart so its letters are rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: Someone takes a needle to get rid of the weeds in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to destroy' shuffles WEEDS into SEWED.
explanation.definitionFit: Stitching with thread is what you do when you have put a needle to work.

clue.text: Foreign king has rest disturbed by revel

parts.note: roi is the French word for king

indicators.note: the word rest is disturbed, its letters thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An overseas monarch's sleep is broken by the noise of partying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign' signals the French word for king; 'disturbed' scrambles the following word, and the scrambled letters come after the king.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse noisily is to make merry, which is what revelling means.

clue.text: Rent trouble gets worker down (with his income ?)

indicators.note: in a down entry this places the worker below the first part
the word Rent is troubled, so its letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: the ant is the crossword's usual worker insect

explanation.surface: A tenant's rent problems leave a working man depressed about his earnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' makes ENTR from RENT, and 'down' puts ANT beneath it. The definition reads 'income' as in-come: someone who comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: A newcomer who goes in is one who has made an 'in-come', an entry, which is the pun the definition rests on.

clue.text: A fair money-spinner ?

parts.note: a fairground attraction that literally spins round and takes the punters' coins

explanation.walkthrough: 'money-spinner' usually means a profitable venture; here the fairground ride spins as well as earning.
explanation.definitionFit: The carousel is a revolving fairground ride, so it both spins and makes money at the fair.

clue.text: Shifting scene it draws

indicators.note: shifting the words scene and it moves their letters into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A changing stage set is what pulls in the crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifting' rearranges SCENE and IT together.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure or tempt someone is to draw them in.

clue.text: It stops the game with the French

parts.note: whist is a card game
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Something brings the match to a halt, along with the French team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the game' looks like part of the definition (a referee's signal), but it supplies WHIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A referee blows this instrument to halt play.

clue.text: Peter, run René around to the undertaker.

indicators.note: running the words around jumbles their letters into another order

explanation.surface: Peter is told to drive René over to the funeral director's.
explanation.walkthrough: The undertaker here is not a funeral director but one who undertakes a business venture; 'around' is the anagram signal, and the accent on René is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who takes on a commercial enterprise is literally one who undertakes it.

clue.text: It's material to many in charge of a duplicate

parts.note: rep is a ribbed fabric
L is the Roman numeral fifty, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: Fabric matters to the many people running a copying business.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact copy of an original is a duplicate.

clue.text: The first carted back to take away

indicators.note: back tells you the whole run, the first letter and the word carted, is read from end to start
the first letter of the word The is taken

parts.note: taken as written; that the reversed run also shows across 'first carted' is a coincidence, since the T comes from the word The

explanation.surface: The leading item was carted back so it could be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the whole of T plus CARTED round, giving DETRAC then T. 'carted' suggests transporting, but it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To detract from something is to diminish or subtract from it.

clue.text: Grand sort of rose, this shrub

parts.note: G is the slang abbreviation for a grand, a thousand

indicators.note: a sort of rose here means the letters of rose remade in another order

explanation.surface: A splendid variety of rose turns out to be this bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' is the anagram signal for the flower's letters; G for grand (a thousand) is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Furze is a spiny yellow-flowered shrub of heathland, also called whin.

clue.text: Song-and-dance girl tends to get ruffled

definitions.text: Song-and-dance girl tends to get ruffled

parts.words: Song-and-dance girl tends to get ruffled
parts.note: a female clown-entertainer of the old seaside concert party, whose costume has a big ruff

explanation.surface: A showgirl is apt to be flustered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruffled' looks like flustered, but the costume of a pierrot's female partner has a large frilled ruff.
explanation.definitionFit: The female counterpart of a pierrot was a singing, dancing performer dressed in a white costume with a ruff.

clue.text: Values properties about one thousand

indicators.note: the properties go about, around, the other letters

parts.note: estates are landed properties
I is the Roman numeral one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A surveyor puts a price on houses at around a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts IM inside ESTATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Approximate valuations are what a surveyor or builder gives as rough prices.

clue.text: Coming again about the electricity

parts.note: re is Latin-derived for about, concerning
a current is a flow of electricity

explanation.surface: Something is coming back to do with the power supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that keeps recurring is happening repeatedly.

clue.text: Painter's lake

parts.note: a lake is a pigment, and the deep red one in a painter's box bears this colour name

explanation.walkthrough: 'lake' is not water but a pigment: crimson lake is a deep red artist's colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimson lake is the name of a red pigment used by artists.

clue.text: Shaped like that little twinkling star?

definitions.text: Shaped like that little twinkling star?

parts.words: Shaped like that little twinkling star
parts.note: the nursery rhyme's star is 'like a diamond in the sky', and a diamond shape is a geometric figure with four equal sides

explanation.surface: A question about having the outline of a tiny glinting star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star' is 'like a diamond in the sky', and the diamond shape is the rhombus.
explanation.definitionFit: A diamond outline is a rhombus, so something diamond-shaped is rhombic.

clue.text: " I see a lily on thy brow, With anguish moist and — dew " (Keats)

definitions.text: I see a lily on thy brow, With anguish moist and — dew

parts.words: I see a lily on thy brow, With anguish moist and — dew
parts.note: the missing word from Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci, describing the sweat of illness on the knight's pale forehead

explanation.walkthrough: The line from Keats's 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' reads 'With anguish moist and fever dew'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem, a high temperature's sweat moistens the knight's lily-white brow.

clue.text: What is imposed outside can alter money matters

indicators.note: the fine goes outside, around, the other letters

parts.note: a fine is a penalty imposed by a court

indicators.note: to alter the word can is to change the order of its letters

explanation.surface: A penalty from outside could change how the money is managed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imposed' points to a penalty; 'outside' wraps that penalty round the scrambled letters given by 'alter'.
explanation.definitionFit: The management of money and funds is what finance means.

clue.text: " That breathes upon a bank of — " (T Night)

definitions.text: That breathes upon a bank of —

parts.words: That breathes upon a bank of
parts.note: the missing word from Orsino's opening speech in Twelfth Night, comparing music to a sweet sound over spring flowers

explanation.walkthrough: 'T Night' is Twelfth Night, whose opening speech has 'the sweet sound That breathes upon a bank of violets'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's line the breeze breathes upon a bank of these purple spring flowers.

clue.text: Dress or undress perhaps

parts.note: in the forces, full ceremonial outfit is called dress and everyday service outfit is called undress

explanation.walkthrough: 'undress' is not nakedness: military 'undress' is the ordinary service uniform, as 'dress' is the ceremonial one.
explanation.definitionFit: Military dress and undress are both kinds of regulation outfit worn by service personnel.

clue.text: Names changed at the minister's house

indicators.note: the word Names is changed by rearranging its letters

explanation.surface: Names were changed at the vicarage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' turns NAMES into MANSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A manse is the residence provided for a Presbyterian or other Nonconformist minister.

clue.text: Scotsman before long gets wind of it

parts.note: mon is the stock Scots form of address 'man'
soon means before long

explanation.surface: A Scot soon hears a rumour about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets wind of' reads as finding out, but 'wind' is the definition: the seasonal wind of South Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: This seasonal wind brings the rainy season to South Asia.

clue.text: Refuse to go into this.

parts.note: read as household rubbish that goes into a receptacle, not as declining to enter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb (decline to go in); it is the noun, rubbish, that goes into a bin.
explanation.definitionFit: Household rubbish is put into this lidded container.

clue.text: Much weight but no sound finish to this part of a car

parts.note: a ton is a heavy weight

indicators.note: the finish of the word is spelt differently but sounds like the clue word no

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like NEAU

explanation.surface: A heavy load, yet no soundproof trim on this bit of the vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: TON comes first; 'sound finish to this' says the rest is spelt NEAU but said like 'no', as in the French-derived word.
explanation.definitionFit: On early cars the tonneau was the rear passenger compartment of the body.

clue.text: Weapons to laugh at explosion, say, in the cold war?

parts.note: a snicker is a sly laugh

indicators.note: say tells you the word is spelt as it sounds

parts.note: a sneeze is the explosion of breath that comes with a cold

explanation.surface: Arms that make a joke of a blast during the frosty stand-off between superpowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the cold' explains the explosion: a sneeze. 'say' means the last part is spelt SNEES but sounds like it. A snickersnee is an old fighting knife.
explanation.definitionFit: A snickersnee is a large knife used for fighting, so the plural names weapons.
